claims.text: The studied material is a dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA produced by additive manufacturing.
The additively manufactured HEA will have better high-temperature oxidation resistance than its cast and wrought counterparts.
Formation of a protective oxide layer will improve the alloy's oxidation resistance.
In situ TEM can elucidate the high-temperature oxidation behavior and nanoprecipitate redistribution in this alloy.
XPS can elucidate the high-temperature oxidation behavior and elemental redistribution in this alloy.
Elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates is mechanistically involved in the alloy's oxidation behavior.
Temperatures above 1000°C are relevant conditions for studying high-temperature oxidation of HEAs.
The relevant service environments include gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components.
The oxidation rate of the additively manufactured alloy will be at least 20% lower than that of cast and wrought counterparts.
Oxidation resistance may vary with the particular additive-manufacturing process and resulting microstructure.
A high-temperature oxidation test can compare oxidation rate and microstructure between additively manufactured and cast or wrought material.
Failure to obtain an oxidation rate at least 20% lower than the cast and wrought controls would falsify the hypothesis.
